name: Kelabit
confidence_why: Blust, the language's principal describer, states plainly in 2013 and 2018 that Kelabit stress is penultimate and shifts rightward to stay penultimate under suffixation, and the only wobble is his own earlier remark (2006, relayed by Hemmings 2016 and Mortensen 2021) that the last two syllables sounded nearly even with a penult preference and that younger speakers and citation forms lean final, which Mortensen 2021 reads as a phrase-final boundary tone laid over regular penultimate stress.

new_statements.quote: The position of stress is far less immediately obvious with some of the more phonologically conservative dialects such as Kemaloh Lun Bawang and Bario Kelabit. [...] Blust (2006:315), dealing with both languages, states that in his original notes (archived as Blust 1971), stress was recorded as being "relatively even on both of the last two syllables, but with a preference for the penult." He contrasts this pattern with audio produced by younger speakers, which "shows a preference for final stress" (ibid.), suggesting that stress patterns may have changed since his original work. A further note states that languages of northern Sarawak commonly appear to have "final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context" (ibid.).

Reading the section around it (lines 2440-2476): Mortensen notes Omar 1983 says only tha…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule (penultimate stress) but qualifies it: the penult preference is mild ('relatively even'), non-contrastive, and apparently drifting to final in younger speakers and in citation forms. The dissertation itself describes Kemaloh Lun Bawang (lund1271), for which Mortensen concludes word-final stress (sec. 3.4, p. 51; 3.4.2.1, p. 55) -- that finding is about Lun Bawang, not Kelabit.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand (Mortensen quoting Blust 2006:315): in Blust's 1971 field notes Bario Kelabit stress is nearly even over the last two syllables with a preference for the penult; younger speakers' recordings prefer final stress; northern Sarawak languages generally show final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context. Stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: Generational drift toward final stress in younger speakers; citation-form final prominence vs. penultimate in phrasal context. Mortensen adds (p. 52-53) that these facts could also be read as regular penultimate stress with a phrase-final boundary tone creating an illusion of final stress, and raises the question of whether Kelabit/Lun Bawang have word-level stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Blust 2001 is about Sa'ban (saba1264), a divergent Dayic relative, not Kelabit; the Blust 2006 remarks (via Mortensen 2021) concern Bario Kelabit specifically, alongside Lun Dayeh/Lun Bawang. Mortensen 2021's own findings describe the Kemaloh dialect of Lun Bawang (lund1271), not Kelabit.

new_statements.quote: 1. STRESS. In PKLD and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban stress is penultimate. In Sa'ban, as just noted, it is generally final, but may be marginally phonemic, depending upon the interpretation of extrametrical schwa in the sequences -/ieC/ and -/ueC/. [p. 267] ... Stress is normally final, but surface contrasts are found in the sequence /ueC/ ... in the sequence /ueC/ the schwa is extrametrical, and stress is normally penultimate. [p. 266, of Sa'ban] ... 5.2.4. Type 4: Syncope of an unstressed vowel. One likely precondition for erosion from the left in Sa'ban was a shift from the PKLD pattern of penultimate word stress to final stress. [p. 288]

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog records Kelabit as penultimate (penultimate stress). Blust's comparative statement that all PKLD descendants other than Sa'ban have penultimate stress covers Kelabit and matches the catalog. The paper's own subject, Sa'ban (saba1265, ISO snv), is described as having final stress; that statement is not about kela1258.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Proto-Kelabit-Lun Dayeh and all its known descendants except Sa'ban (hence Kelabit, including Bario Kelabit, the reference dialect used throughout the paper), word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Sa'ban itself (a different Glottolog language, saba1265) innovated final stress, with a marginal penultimate/final surface contrast in -ieC/-ueC sequences where the schwa is extrametrical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress for Kelabit or PKLD. (p. 260/PDF 12 calls prepenultimate syllables 'pretonic', consistent with penultimate main stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kelabit. For Sa'ban only: extrametrical schwa in -/ieC/, -/ueC/ yields penultimate stress there, with rare oxytone contrasts written /uweC/ vs /ueC/ (e.g. /luek/ 'spoon' vs /luwek/ 'chest').
new_statements.identity_note: The work's subject is Sa'ban (Glottolog saba1265, ISO 639-3 snv), which Blust treats lexicostatistically as a divergent dialect of Kelabit-Lun Dayeh but which Glottolog lists as a separate language. The Kelabit data cited in the paper are Bario Kelabit (bari1288, the prestige dialect). The stress statement usable for kela1258 is the comparative generalization over 'PKLD and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban'.

readall_conflicts: The single listed work (Blust 2001, Sa'ban) could not be downloaded (sealang.net port 80 refused; https self-signed certificate), so no new primary statement on Kelabit was opened. The only Kelabit-specific evidence held by the project is second-hand: Mortensen 2021 (p. 52) quoting Blust 2006:315, which reports a mild penult preference in 1971 notes but a final-stress preference in younger speakers and in citation forms, and Mortensen's own reading that the citation-form final prominence may be a boundary-tone effect over regular penultimate stress. This is compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule but shows the placement is weak, non-contrastive and possibly changing; it is not a clean contradiction. Mortensen's own conclusion of word-final stress applies to Kemaloh Lun Bawang, not Kelabit.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every deciding sentence is verbatim in the held Blust 2018 (p.5) and Blust 2013 (pp.256-257, 738) text files at the stated locators. The classification (penultimate, weight-blind, rightward shift under suffixation; schwa+flap exception) rests on explicit statements by the language's principal describer in 2013 and 2018, so nothing held contradicts the classification of lexical stress. Two gaps keep it short of well-sourced: (a) the dedicated phonology article Blust 2016 (OL 55:246-277) is not yet obtained and is closed-access (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar report no OA copy; MUSE blocked); (b) the held Hemmings 2016 grammar (p.103) records a competing statement, that Asmah 1983:551 and Blust 2006:315 give final stress in citation form with Blust distinguishing lexical from phrasal stress, and neither of those sources is.
